subject: differences in using JAGS and WinBUGS

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: differences in using JAGS and WinBUGS
parts:
Dear all,

 

a colleague just asked me about the differences between running WinBUGS and JAGS from R. Here is a non-exhaustive list of things.

A typical call to WinBUGS via bugs() in R2WinBUGS looks like this:

out <- bugs(data, inits, parameters, "model.txt", n.thin = nt,

n.chains = nc, n.burnin = nb, n.iter = ni, debug = TRUE,

bugs.directory = bd)   # with bd defined appropriately

A typical call to JAGS via jags() from jagsUI looks like this:

out <- jags(data, inits, parameters, "model.txt", n.thin=nt,

   n.chains = nc, n.burnin = nb, n.iter = ni)

That is, all is the same except for the last two args in bugs, which don't exist in jags.

Otherwise, there are a couple of minor differences in the BUGS dialect as implemented in WinBUGS and JAGS. These are fairly minor though

Finally, the biggest difference in practice, in my opinion, is that JAGS is MUCH more iffy with initial values. Basically, JAGS does not forgive any conflict between initials, data and model. That means that when a chain for the latent presence-absence state z in an occupancy model is initialzed at z = 0, and the data contain a 1 for that site (i.e., the species was seen at least once), then JAGS will crash, because under the standard model, without false positives, this is impossible.

In the case of simple occupancy models, it is fairly easy to avoid trouble here, but with more complex models with multiple states for instance, it may be very difficult to find sets of inits that do not derail JAGS. In practice, this is one of the main drawbacks of JAGS in my view.

Kind regards  --- Marc
